nameStory: Alsike clover gets its name from the town of Alsike in Sweden, where this European native was first cultivated and studied. Swedish botanists developed this hardy clover variety in the 1700s, and farmers found it so useful that it spread across the world. The name stuck even as the plant naturalized far from its Swedish homeland!
description: Alsike clover is a medium-sized wildflower that looks like a cross between red and white clover. It grows up to about 16 inches tall with the classic three-leaflet clover leaves and round, puffy flower heads. The flowers start out white but blush to soft pink as they age, creating pretty two-toned clusters. You'll often find it mixed in with grasses in fields, along roadsides, and in meadows throughout New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Round, globe-shaped flower heads about the size of a marble, starting white and aging to pale pink. The flowers feel soft and papery when touched, and individual tiny flowers point in all directions from a central stalk that rises above the leaves.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Classic three-part clover leaves that are unmarked - no white chevrons or spots like some other clovers. The leaflets feel smooth and thin, oval-shaped with finely toothed edges that you can feel if you run your finger along them.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in an upright, branching pattern rather than creeping along the ground. The stems feel hollow and somewhat weak, often leaning against neighboring plants for support in dense patches.

idTips.label: Flower Stalks
idTips.description: Flower heads sit on distinct stalks that emerge from where leaves meet the stem (leaf axils). These stalks are usually longer than the leaves, holding the flowers up and away from the foliage.

habitat: Alsike clover thrives in moist, fertile soils and is commonly found in fields, meadows, roadsides, and disturbed areas throughout New England. It prefers slightly acidic to neutral soils and can tolerate wetter conditions than many other clovers. You'll often spot it mixed with grasses and other wildflowers in abandoned agricultural areas and along the edges of wetlands.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges in early spring with fresh three-part leaves. First flowers may appear by late spring in warmer areas, starting as pure white rounded heads.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with abundant white-to-pink flower heads throughout the summer months. This is the best time for identification as flowers and leaves are both fully developed.
seasonality.fall: Continues blooming into early fall with flower heads showing more pink coloration. Seeds develop in small pods, and plants may produce new growth flushes after summer heat breaks.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level in harsh New England winters. Only dried stems and seed heads may remain visible above snow, making identification difficult until spring regrowth.

funFact: Alsike clover is actually toxic to horses, causing a condition called 'alsike poisoning' that makes horses sensitive to sunlight and can cause severe skin damage on white or light-colored areas of their bodies - yet it's perfectly safe for cattle and other livestock to eat!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with white clover, but alsike grows upright rather than creeping, has stalked flower heads (white clover flowers sit directly on the stem), and its flowers age to pink. Remember: 'Alsike stands up, white clover crawls around.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name suggesting it's a hybrid (the scientific name 'hybridum'), alsike clover is actually a distinct species, not a cross between other clovers. Early botanists thought it looked intermediate between red and white clover and mistakenly assumed it was a natural hybrid.
compareHints: Among New England's clovers, alsike is the tall one with color-changing flowers. Red clover has larger, deeper pink-purple flowers and fuzzy leaves, while white clover creeps along the ground. The various hop clovers have yellow flowers in small, tight clusters rather than the round, puffy heads of alsike.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's clovers, red clover is the tallest and most upright, while white clover creeps along the ground and has white flowers.
Among New England clovers, white clover is unique for its creeping growth habit and pure white spherical flowers.

Among New England clovers, rabbitfoot clover is unique for its fuzzy, pale, cylindrical flower heads - completely different from the round pink heads of red clover, the round white heads of white clover, or the small yellow clusters of hop clovers.
Among New England's yellow-flowered clovers, large hop clover stands tallest and most erect, while hop trefoil sprawls closer to the ground with smaller flowers.

Among New England's yellow-flowered clovers, hop trefoil stands out with its distinctive oval, hop-shaped flower heads compared to the round heads of large hop clover or the tiny heads of lesser hop trefoil.
Among New England's clovers, lesser hop trefoil stands out for its tiny size and bright yellow flowers - most other clovers have white, pink, or red blooms.
Crimson clover stands out from other New England clovers by its distinctive torpedo-shaped, brilliant red flower heads - no other local clover has this intense crimson color or elongated cone shape.
Zigzag clover differs from red clover by having narrower leaflets without white markings and distinctive angled stems.
